title: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease (GTD) is an abnormal proliferation of trophoblast cells. It encompasses hydatidiform moles, invasive moles, and choriocarcinoma, all producing hCG and varying in malignancy.

sections.p: GTD refers to a spectrum of placental tumours arising from abnormal proliferation of trophoblast cells. It includes hydatidiform mole (complete or partial), invasive mole, and choriocarcinoma. Diagnosis is suspected with abnormal uterine bleeding in pregnancy, excessively high hCG levels, or a uterus larger than dates.

GTD is staged using the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) staging system, which considers tumour location, size, and presence of metastases. Prognostic scoring systems, like the WHO system, incorporate factors such as age, hCG levels, uterine size, and presence of metastases to predict outcome.
b: Stage II: extends outside uterus but confined to pelvis.
Stage IV: distant metastases (brain, liver, etc.).

sections.p: The exact cause is unknown, but it's linked to abnormal fertilization. Risk factors include extremes of maternal age (under 20 or over 35) and previous GTD. In low-resource settings, consider that some herbal remedies might interfere with diagnosis or management.

Patients typically present with vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy, often heavier than expected for gestational age. Other symptoms include hyperemesis gravidarum, passage of molar tissue, and signs of hyperthyroidism. Some may present with symptoms of metastasis.

t.b: To detect pregnancy and monitor GTD. Markedly elevated levels suggest GTD. Serial measurements are crucial for diagnosis and follow-up.
To visualize the uterus and identify molar tissue or a non-viable pregnancy. A 'snowstorm' appearance is characteristic of a complete mole. Helps rule out ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage.
To assess for anaemia from bleeding and monitor general health. Important before potential chemotherapy.
To assess for organ involvement, especially if metastases are suspected or before chemotherapy.
To screen for pulmonary metastases, a common site for choriocarcinoma spread.

sections.p: Severe vaginal bleeding, signs of pulmonary embolism, neurological deficits (suggesting brain metastases), or acute respiratory distress are critical red flags. Complications include haemorrhage, uterine perforation, and development of persistent GTD or choriocarcinoma.

The primary treatment is evacuation of the uterus, usually by suction curettage, followed by histological confirmation. Chemotherapy is indicated for persistent GTD or choriocarcinoma. Methotrexate is the first-line agent due to its efficacy and lower toxicity compared to alternatives.
b: Hysterectomy may be considered in specific cases.

sections.p: Close follow-up with serial hCG monitoring is essential to detect recurrence or persistent disease. Contraception is vital to prevent pregnancy during follow-up, as pregnancy can interfere with hCG monitoring. Counselling on recurrence risk is important.
b: Serial hCG monitoring until undetectable for 3 consecutive weeks.

sections.p: GTD can be mistaken for miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or normal pregnancy with complications like hyperemesis or pre-eclampsia due to overlapping symptoms like vaginal bleeding and elevated hCG.
b: Molar degeneration of the placenta (part of GTD spectrum).

sections.p: hCG levels can be falsely elevated by exogenous hCG injections or certain tumours. Ultrasound may be non-diagnostic in early stages or if there are co-existing conditions. A normal-sized uterus with bleeding can mask GTD.
b: hCG can be elevated in normal pregnancy, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy.
Ultrasound may not be definitive for early or partial moles.
Normal uterine size does not exclude GTD.

faq.q: What is the main difference between a complete and partial mole?
faq.a: A complete mole has only paternal chromosomes, while a partial mole has both maternal and paternal chromosomes, often with a co-existing fetus.

faq.q: Why is contraception important after GTD?
faq.a: Pregnancy can raise hCG levels, masking persistent GTD and complicating monitoring. It also increases the risk of recurrence.

faq.q: Can GTD occur after a normal pregnancy?
faq.a: Yes, though rarely, GTD can occur after a term pregnancy, miscarriage, or abortion.
